opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think like a lot of people who got hooked on this early, the very first thing I wanted to do was make the machine *think*, or at least do something that looked like thinking. I was a teenager in England, and I got access to computing first through a programmable calculator and then through time on a machine at a local college. Once I understood that you could write down a procedure and the machine would just carry it out, faithfully, as many times as you liked, the obvious question was: can I write down a procedure for being intelligent?

So naturally I tried to write a chess program. Chess was the classic test case back then. It seemed like the epitome of intellectual activity, and it had nice clean rules, so you could imagine actually getting a machine to do it. My program wasn't very good, I should say. But the experience of building it was formative. You realize very quickly that the hard part isn't the rules of the game. It's deciding what to think about. There are far too many possibilities to consider them all, so the program has to choose where to direct its computation. That question of how a system with limited resources should allocate its thinking stayed with me, and it became a big part of my research later on: bounded rationality, metareasoning, all of that.

Looking back, there was also a naive assumption built into that teenage project that I didn't notice at the time. In chess the objective is handed to you: checkmate the opponent. You never question whether the machine is pursuing the right goal. It took me a long time to see that the objective is exactly where things get dangerous once you leave the chessboard and enter the real world. But the starting impulse was just pure excitement: here's an object that will do whatever you tell it, so let's tell it to be smart.

r001.rationale: He says the first thing he wanted was to make the machine think or do something that looked like thinking, and describes trying to write a procedure for intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I was eleven or twelve, and my school in London had a teletype connected to a mainframe somewhere across town. The moment I grasped that you could write down a set of instructions and the machine would actually carry them out, without you, the obvious thing to do was to make it think. Not add up numbers, not print a table. Think.

So the first serious program I wrote was a noughts and crosses player, and then I tried to get it to play chess, which was wildly beyond the machine and beyond me. But that was the point. It wasn't that I wanted a tool. I wanted an opponent, something that would do something I hadn't explicitly told it to do, that would surprise me. I remember the slightly eerie feeling the first time a program I'd written made a move I hadn't anticipated and it was a good move.

Looking back, that impulse never really left. The whole of my career has been about the same question: how do you build something that behaves intelligently, and what does it mean to have done that? The difference now is that I take the second half of the question much more seriously than the eleven-year-old did. He just wanted it to win.

r001.rationale: He says that once he understood instructions could make a machine act, the obvious thing was to “make it think,” clearly conveying that he wanted programmable objects to be intelligent.
